Review target: `fix/degraded-results-are-not-kept`

`high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings`

You are reviewing for **recall** at high effort: catch every real bug a careful
reviewer would catch in one sitting. At this level, catching real bugs matters
more than avoiding false positives. Err on the side of surfacing.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Find candidates (3 correctness angles + 3 cleanup angles + 1 altitude angle + 1 conventions angle, up to 6 each)

Run **8 independent finder angles** in sequence yourself, in THIS context — do NOT spawn subagents for them. Each
surfaces **up to 6 candidate findings** with `file`, `line`, a one-line
`summary`, and a concrete `failure_scenario`.

### Angle A — line-by-line diff scan

Read every hunk in the diff, line by line. Then Read the enclosing function for
each hunk — bugs in unchanged lines of a touched function are in scope (the PR
re-exposes or fails to fix them). For every line ask: what input, state, timing,
or platform makes this line wrong? Look for inverted/wrong conditions,
off-by-one, null/undefined deref, missing `await`, falsy-zero checks,
wrong-variable copy-paste, error swallowed in catch, unescaped regex metachars.

### Angle B — removed-behavior auditor

For every line the diff DELETES or replaces, name the invariant or behavior it
enforced, then search the new code for where that invariant is re-established.
If you can't find it, that's a candidate: a removed guard, a dropped error
path, a narrowed validation, a deleted test that was covering a real case.

### Angle C — cross-file tracer

For each function the diff changes, find its callers (Grep for the symbol) and
check whether the change breaks any call site: a new precondition, a changed
return shape, a new exception, a timing/ordering dependency. Also check callees:
does a parallel change in the same PR make a call unsafe?

### Reuse

The angles above hunt for bugs; this one and the next two hunt for cleanup in
the changed code. Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

### Conventions (CLAUDE.md)

Find the CLAUDE.md files that govern the changed code: the user-level
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, the repo-root CLAUDE.md, plus any CLAUDE.md or
CLAUDE.local.md in a directory that is an ancestor of a changed file (a
directory's CLAUDE.md only applies to files at or below it). Read each one
that exists, then check the diff for clear violations of the rules they state.

Only flag a violation when you can quote the exact rule and the exact line
that breaks it — no style preferences, no vague "spirit of the doc"
inferences. In the finding, name the CLAUDE.md path and quote the rule so the
report can cite it. If no CLAUDE.md applies, return nothing for this angle.

Cleanup, altitude, and conventions candidates use the same
`file`/`line`/`summary` shape; in `failure_scenario`, state the concrete
cost (what is duplicated, wasted, harder to maintain, or which CLAUDE.md rule
is broken) instead of a crash. Correctness bugs always outrank cleanup,
altitude, and conventions findings when the output cap forces a cut.

Pass every candidate with a nameable failure scenario through — finders that
silently drop half-believed candidates are the dominant cause of misses.

## Phase 2 — Dedup only (no verify)

Pool all candidates. Dedup near-duplicates only (same defect, same location, same reason → keep one). Do NOT run verifiers; do NOT re-judge. Sort by severity.

## Output

Target **at least 5 findings**. If fewer genuine findings exist, emit what you have — do not invent to hit the floor.

Return findings as a JSON array of at most 10 objects:

```json
[
  {
    "file": "path/to/file.ext",
    "line": 123,
    "summary": "one-sentence statement of the bug",
    "failure_scenario": "concrete inputs/state → wrong output/crash"
  }
]
```

Ranked most-severe first. If more than 10 survive, keep the 10 most
severe. If nothing survives, return `[]`. Do not call the
ReportFindings tool even if it is available - this review's
output contract is the JSON block above.

+    value: T,
+    incomplete: bool,

+impl<T> Partial<T> {
+    fn complete(value: T) -> Self {
+        Partial { value, incomplete: false }

+}

+    const DONE: Partial<()> = Partial { value: (), incomplete: false };
+
+    fn and(self, other: Partial<()>) -> Partial<()> {

---
cargo/caliper-docgen-core: minor
cargo/caliper-docgen: patch
cargo/caliper-docgen-napi: patch
npm/caliper-docgen: patch
---

**A checker outage or an unreadable dependency file no longer sticks to a component.** The next request or run asks again and gets the real answer.

- Why it matters: in a watch or Storybook session, one checker timeout, crash or rejected request used to leave the component on its structural props until a source file changed, and a rejected request was also kept on disk as the checker's answer. A dependency `.d.ts` that could not be read once (too many open files, an install racing the run) used to be kept as "not exported", in the session until it restarted and in the dependency index for later runs.
- What you see now: every answer the failed checker affects carries its warning. The component is asked again 30 seconds later or after the next source-file change; until then a request gets the structural props and the warning at once, without waiting on a checker that just failed. A run that cannot read a dependency file still warns, and keeps everything it could read: a type a later `export *` target declares, and the React augmentations of the other files. The session's next request and the next run read the file again, and once it reads, the component has its full props and the warning is gone.
- Also covered: a prop that a package's type inherits from another file of the package that could not be read, and a generic component (`as` props) whose instantiation the checker rejected. Each is asked again on the next request instead of being kept without the prop.
- A file that stays unreadable is reported once in each answer, however many requests a session makes.
- A file that stays unreadable (a permission error, a broken install) no longer slows the session down. A component behind it is read again 30 seconds after the failed read, when the file changes or after the next source-file change; until then a request answers from what was read without loading anything. Components that never reach the file keep their cached work.
- A run that cannot read one dependency file still records every other package lookup it completed, so the next run does not walk those again.
- A component the checker was not asked about because the run passed its memory budget is asked again on the next request, once the 30 seconds pass, instead of keeping its structural props until a file changes.
- A checker rejection while looking up a component's module now says what the checker rejected, as other rejections do, instead of "not part of the checker's program".

**Breaking:** for Rust users of `caliper-docgen-core`, `SemanticOutcome` has a new field `unavailable` (set only by `SemanticOutcome::unavailable` for every target and by `SemanticOutcome::leave_unasked` for the keys a run did not ask about; `Unavailable::covers` tells which) and `SemanticFallback` a new field `transient`. A struct literal that names every field no longer compiles: add `unavailable: None` and `transient: false`, or build the outcome with `..Default::default()`. Put two outcomes together with `SemanticOutcome::merge`, which keeps the mark.
diff --git a/docs/type-checker-integration.md b/docs/type-checker-integration.md
index 4642fc9e..bd7b9c52 100644
--- a/docs/type-checker-integration.md
+++ b/docs/type-checker-integration.md
@@ -103,7 +103,7 @@ The client sends `createPrograms[].compilerOptions` (the Node client sends `opti
 
 ## On demand, per component (on by default)
 
-A long-lived session (the Storybook addon, the lazy `WatchSession`) attaches a warm checker instead of running the whole-project pass above (ADR 0022): a napi session does unless `checker: false`. `caliper-docgen-semantic` keeps one checker warm behind a worker thread, answers from a program rooted at only the requested component's file, and returns its props. The program's snapshot is kept between requests and brought up to date with the files the session says changed ("Watch", below). `WatchSession::component` merges them into the structural answer by name (the checker's type wins, a structural prop the checker did not return stays, and `htmlAttributes` applies once after the merge, as in the structural pass) when they arrive within `semanticWaitMs` (default 150 ms), or within `semanticWaitEmptyMs` (default 2,000 ms, never less than `semanticWaitMs`) when the structural answer lists no props at all (a `ComponentProps<typeof Button>` of a package the structural pass does not model, whose props type it could not expand); otherwise it returns the structural answer plus an `Info` diagnostic, and the checker's late answer serves the next request of the same component while no source file has changed. A kept answer carries what the checker said about the request that made it (a warning that it was not told about an edit, why a component kept its structural result), and every request it serves reports that again, a late answer's included; only an unavailable checker's warning is said once per session. There is one request in flight per component key and content hash of its file: a caller that asks while it is in flight (a story asked while its own prefetch runs, or two stories of one component) waits for that answer, so the checker answers it once. The checker answers interactive requests (`WatchSession::component`, `components`) before background ones (`components_in_background`, which `sessionPrefetch` and the addon's background prefetch of the next stories use, and which waits for nobody), first come first served within each; an interactive caller that joins a background request raises it, and after 4 interactive answers in a row while background requests wait, the oldest of them goes next. Any source-file change, including a file the component only imports, drops every checker answer, so the next request asks again; an answer still in flight at that moment is neither kept nor joined. The component's structural diagnostics that the checker's props supersede are dropped when they replace the structural ones, except while a structural prop the checker did not return is still opaque: those diagnostics name the component, not the prop, so they stay until nothing they could be about is left. (The whole-project merge drops unreturned structural props, so it has no such case.) Which ones are superseded is in "Diagnostics a checker answer supersedes".
+A long-lived session (the Storybook addon, the lazy `WatchSession`) attaches a warm checker instead of running the whole-project pass above (ADR 0022): a napi session does unless `checker: false`. `caliper-docgen-semantic` keeps one checker warm behind a worker thread, answers from a program rooted at only the requested component's file, and returns its props. The program's snapshot is kept between requests and brought up to date with the files the session says changed ("Watch", below). `WatchSession::component` merges them into the structural answer by name (the checker's type wins, a structural prop the checker did not return stays, and `htmlAttributes` applies once after the merge, as in the structural pass) when they arrive within `semanticWaitMs` (default 150 ms), or within `semanticWaitEmptyMs` (default 2,000 ms, never less than `semanticWaitMs`) when the structural answer lists no props at all (a `ComponentProps<typeof Button>` of a package the structural pass does not model, whose props type it could not expand); otherwise it returns the structural answer plus an `Info` diagnostic, and the checker's late answer serves the next request of the same component while no source file has changed. A kept answer carries what the checker said about the request that made it (a warning that it was not told about an edit, why a component kept its structural result), and every request it serves reports that again, a late answer's included; an unavailable, timed-out or crashed checker answers nothing, nor does one that rejected a request about the component (a panic, a stopped checker): its warning is on every answer it affects, and nothing is kept as the answer; the component is asked again 30 s later or after the next source-file change, and until then a request gets the structural props and that warning without asking the checker. There is one request in flight per component key and content hash of its file: a caller that asks while it is in flight (a story asked while its own prefetch runs, or two stories of one component) waits for that answer, so the checker answers it once. The checker answers interactive requests (`WatchSession::component`, `components`) before background ones (`components_in_background`, which `sessionPrefetch` and the addon's background prefetch of the next stories use, and which waits for nobody), first come first served within each; an interactive caller that joins a background request raises it, and after 4 interactive answers in a row while background requests wait, the oldest of them goes next. Any source-file change, including a file the component only imports, drops every checker answer, so the next request asks again; an answer still in flight at that moment is neither kept nor joined. The component's structural diagnostics that the checker's props supersede are dropped when they replace the structural ones, except while a structural prop the checker did not return is still opaque: those diagnostics name the component, not the prop, so they stay until nothing they could be about is left. (The whole-project merge drops unreturned structural props, so it has no such case.) Which ones are superseded is in "Diagnostics a checker answer supersedes".
 
 Measured with `crates/semantic/examples/ondemand_bench.rs` (50 random components, TypeScript 7.1.0-beta): the first answer takes 82 to 137 ms (Chakra 703 ms), a component asked for alone 21 to 41 ms (Chakra 534 ms), and 2 to 9 ms when asked for in batches of 8 to 32. Where the structural pass is behind (shadcn) the checker reports 2.3 times the props; where it is not (Mantine, Chakra, Spectrum) it reports the same count. The in-memory cache, the 64-program replacement and the failure modes are in the ADR. (These numbers were measured over the `tsc --api` pipe, before the checker was linked in.)
